newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-COMMERCIAL UNION RULES OUT MERGER.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-COMMERCIAL UNION RULES OUT MERGER.

text.p: British composite insurance group Commercial Union on Wednesday ruled out any possibility of a merger and said it expected its life business would expand at a faster rate than general insurance in the future.
With its recent pick-up of a majority in Union Financiere de France, the proportion of Commercial Union's life business as part of its total business had risen from 45 to 50 percent.

But Peter Foster, Commercial Union's finance director ruled out any possible merger with either ABN AMRO or the insurance business owned by B.A.T Industries , rumours of which have swung back and forth in the market.
Foster said Commercial Union was on the lookout for further takeovers in the life sector -- considered to be more lucrative than general insurance -- both in eastern and western Europe.
"The life market will tend to grow more quickly and therefore one would expect to see our life business grow at a faster rate than our general insurance and that applies across the group," he said.

Foster was speaking after the insurer reported a 8.8 percent rise in pre-tax operating profits to 235 million pounds in six months to June, 1997, which at constant exchange rates reflected a rise of 25 percent.
"We do believe we have a very strong business and we do not believe we have to do anything in terms of consolidating or merging with another company," he said.
"Overall, we do not believe that we need to merge with anybody else. We (also) do not believe that we need to make a major acquisition of that kind," he said.
The restructuring of Commercial Union's non-life business in the UK was on track to produce some 100 million pounds of savings annually by 1999.

The group is also expecting to tighten its belt in France where life business has been sluggish due to political and economic uncertainties. Commercial Union has reorganised its sales force in France, considered a major life market in Europe.
"It may not be until before 1998 that one would really see business moving strongly ahead (in France)," Foster said.
He also expected rates to firm up further and said there had been cases where some of Commercial Union's competitors were raising rates to its levels.
"I would say that rates are bumping along the bottom and I would expect the next move in the upward direction," he said.
